title: True sun and place for the devil; work, speech, Spirit, seal (Eph 4:26–31)
english: “the sun will go down on your prophets at noon,” so too it goes down on all who sin, and no longer grants them its own rising while they go on sinning. So Paul commands us not to do such things in anger that the sun goes down on us and night comes into our souls.

“And do not give place to the devil” (Ephesians 4:27). Origen says: this is like what is said in Ecclesiastes: “If the spirit of the ruler rises up against you, do not leave your place, for healing puts an end to great sins” (Ecclesiastes 10:4). We give place to the devil, or to the ruling spirit when it has risen up against us, whenever our governing faculty has not been filled with holy teachings, or with saving faith and with thoughts that discern and counsel us what is best. For, according to Zechariah the father of John, Satan settles on the regions of the soul; and such assents to what is worse, and leanings toward those assents, invite the devil to come into our souls. So too it is written of Judas the traitor: first, that the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, to betray him (John 13:2), and after this, that after the morsel Satan entered into him (John 13:27). So if, when the devil had put it into Judas’s heart to betray the Lord, Judas had stood against what was put there, Satan would not afterward have found a place to enter him.

“Let him who steals steal no longer; rather let him labor, working with his hands what is good, so that he may have something to share with one in need” (Ephesians 4:28). Many of those who are thought to have believed are busy with the affairs of life, and on the pretext of providing for their needs, even if they seem to be clean of idolatry and of all fornication, they do not easily keep from stealing when they buy and sell and do business with others. For this reason he did not hesitate to reproach them, as though some were still stealing (and this in Ephesus), as one who knew people of this kind. The very words “working what is good” point to an honest livelihood. Those who make their living unjustly work not what is good but what is evil; those who reverently secure what they need work what is good in this as well.

“Let no rotten word come out of your mouth, but whatever is good for building up as the need requires, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4:29). Origen says: the good word, which builds up as the need requires and gives grace to those who hear, is the word that teaches, that urges toward virtue and draws away from vice. The rotten word is the one that feeds vice and stirs people up toward what is worse.

“And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Ephesians 4:30). Grief is a passion, and it is rightly defined as “a fresh opinion that evil is present, at which it is fitting to shrink.” But the Holy Spirit does not form opinions, nor (granting that it does) does it hold the opinion that evil is present to it. If that is so, the Holy Spirit will not be grieved. Is it, then, that as far as it rests with us, we grieve the Holy Spirit of God when we do these things? The Lord too says in Ezekiel, “And in all these things you grieved me” (Ezekiel 16:43). What we have often said about anger and wrath, about sleep and about words that speak of God in human feelings, is useful also for the discussion of “do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God.”

We were sealed with the Holy Spirit so that, receiving the stamp of the Holy Spirit while the one who sealed remains undivided, and taking the impressions of the Holy Spirit, we may become holy; and so that the spirit of the man that is in each of us may become holy, and, I think, the soul as well. The one who is sealed, then, is sealed with the Holy Spirit, but God is the one who seals. Everyone who, by believing God, has set his seal to this, that God is true (John 3:33), is sealed by the Father with the Holy Spirit; and he is sealed so that, by keeping the seal and showing it unbroken on the day of redemption, he may be counted among the redeemed.

“Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and blasphemy be put away from you, with all malice” (Ephesians 4:31). Origen says: some have thought anger to be a generic passion, while placing it in turn under the genus of desire; and they have given this definition of anger: “Anger is a desire to punish one who seems to have done wrong improperly.” They list many species of anger, and among them they rank bitterness, as anger that is hard to receive or that bursts out at once (they say “hard to receive” is taken

title: Bitterness, wrath, anger, clamor, blasphemy; kindness and forgiving (Eph 4:31–32)
english: in the sense that it is not easy for those outside to accept), and wrath as anger in its beginning. Scripture seems in very many places to know a difference between wrath and anger, as in “Lord, do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor discipline me in your anger.” Yet we will not define in the same way the wrath of God that rebukes and the wrath that must be put away from us, nor the anger of the Lord that disciplines and our own. For what is said of God is said more figuratively, while what is named in us is, by common consent, passions and sins.

The word bitterness occurs also in Jeremiah: “And your bitterness,” he says, “has come up to me.” So I think the apostle is now speaking of bitterness in the sense in which we call some people bitter, the opposite of sweet; for common usage knows both sweet people and bitter ones. Wrath is the anger that is beginning to arise in the soul at something; and anger, perhaps, is not the genus of these and of others like them, but anger already ready and active for “the punishment of one thought to have done wrong.” And clamor, as a rule, follows these passions too: the bitter, the wrathful and the angry shout, and speak more noisily, and bring out words of bitterness, wrath and anger. So, in addition to the former, we must also train ourselves to have clamor put away from us.

The blasphemy here, which he commands to be put away from us, is, I think, what people often bring out from passion when they are angry, people who in the moment of anger dare to speak even against the divine; and blasphemy is again taken to cover every accusation against anyone at all, since those who speak ill of others are said to blaspheme those they speak ill of. So, following the words about bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor, it is said that blasphemy too must be put away.

If, however, we were also to class as blasphemy every utterance that speaks ill of the divine, not only when people speak evil out of grief and anger in times of displeasure, but often also from ignorance of the teaching of the truth, as is clear from the doctrines held among the heterodox, then the one who declares the true teaching false, or the false true, blasphemes too, above all about God and the things of God. Who, then, is so approved a money-changer as to know how to test everything, to hold fast to what is good and to keep away from every form of evil (1 Thessalonians 5:21–22)?

Some think that anger sometimes arises with good reason. They wrongly add to the gospel the words “without cause” in the saying “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5:22); for some have read “whoever is angry with his brother without cause.” Let us put them to shame with the present text, which says, “Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and blasphemy be put away from you.” For here the word “all” is plainly said in common of them all, so that no bitterness is allowed, no wrath is permitted, and no anger comes upon us with good reason. And in Psalm 37, as though all anger were sin (and wrath likewise), it is said, “Cease from anger and forsake wrath” (Psalm 37:8). So it is never reasonable to be angry with anyone. And we must work hard to have put away from us not only all bitterness and all wrath and all anger and all blasphemy, but these together with all malice; and by malice we understand either the state opposed to virtue, or wickedness.

“Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving yourselves, as God in Christ also forgave us” (Ephesians 4:32). Origen says: we named sweet as the opposite of bitter; but Paul seems now to call kindness what stands opposite bitterness, by a metaphor taken from foods. So we can understand “Be kind to one another” as meaning “people easy to approach, sweet and gentle in character.” This happens if we put away harshness, mercilessness and want of sympathy toward our neighbor and become tenderhearted toward all; and by this we give the greatest gifts not only to those near us but also to ourselves. For “forgiving yourselves” is something other than “forgiving one another,” since whatever good we do to others when we benefit them returns to ourselves, both because of its end and because we are of one body, more than to those we seem to have helped. And we give ourselves all that God also gave us in Christ, as it were receiving these gifts, keeping them, and imitating the Giver and his way of giving. title: Forgiveness in Christ; sexual vices named; inheritance (Eph 4:32–5:5)
english: another,” will think it is said with the same force as “forgiving one another,” chiefly because of “as God in Christ forgave us,” and will refer these words to the forgiveness of sins, saying that we must forgive those who sin against us, as God also forgave us our sins. But how did God in Christ forgive us our sins? Is it because the Father, being in Christ, forgave us our trespasses? Yet in Christ he also gave us good things, if indeed in Christ is the wisdom that he gave us, and truth and righteousness.

“But fornication and all uncleanness or greed must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints; nor shamefulness and foolish talk or jesting, which are not fitting, but rather thanksgiving” (Ephesians 5:3–4). Origen says: by the custom of Scripture, intercourse with a prostitute is called fornication; but every sin in the region of fleshly titillation, not only adulteries and the corruption of boys but also all the other things that human licentiousness has devised in varied and manifold rubbings, has been named, as a class, uncleanness.

Greed must be understood either more simply or, as we have shown elsewhere, as adultery, where we also used the words “that no one go beyond and overreach his brother” (1 Thessalonians 4:6). All uncleanness must be guarded against, since this is what is fitting for saints. There is a kind of shamefulness in each form of licentiousness; and in the same way shamefulness is also uncleanness, for every act in the region whose work is excretion shows both the unclean and the shameful. But this must be said of acts against nature, not of marriage.

Let us see also what foolish talk is, which itself, too, must not even be named among the saints. Someone who takes the word more simply will say that foolish talk is what buffoons and jesters practice. But see whether we must not also say that all who are in any way estranged from wisdom and understanding talk foolishly, and that what they lay down as doctrine is foolish. The jesting that is joined to foolish talk will seem to agree with taking foolish talk more simply, for the usage of ordinary people applies the word to those who raise a laugh not only from foolish talk but from any cause at all. This too is not fitting for saints, but rather thanksgiving to God in all things, or else a “thanksgiving” that means grace, as when we call people gracious and charming.

So one must not be a foolish talker and a jester, but gracious and charming. And since it is unusual to say “but rather graciousness,” perhaps he used instead the word that belongs to something else and said “but rather thanksgiving.” Perhaps, too, those who come from the Hebrews are accustomed to use the words “thanksgiving” and “thankful” for “graciousness” and “gracious.” We thought that what is said in Proverbs is of this kind: “A thankful woman raises up glory for her husband,” in place of “a gracious woman.” But we would have seemed to force the text in taking “a thankful woman” as “a gracious woman,” if the other versions did not agree with this reading. For Aquila translated, “A woman of grace holds fast to glory,” and Theodotion and Symmachus, “A woman of grace will hold fast to glory” (Proverbs 11:16).

“For know this, that every fornicator or unclean or greedy person, who is an idolater, has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God” (Ephesians 5:5). We must observe that, having forbidden six sins (fornication, uncleanness, greed, shamefulness, foolish talk and jesting), he does not add of all six that whoever is guilty of any of them has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God, but of three, I mean fornication, all uncleanness and greed. For if the one guilty of foolish talk and jesting also had no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God, the judgment would seem to some rather harsh, since it would pardon our weak nature in nothing. These things are not fitting either, it is true; but not so that by doing them anyone falls from the inheritance of Christ and God.

It remains to consider shamefulness as well. You might think it reasonable to say, “every fornicator or unclean or greedy or shameful person has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.” But perhaps shamefulness lies in the one who has been stained by passion only in secret, in which state a person, even when inflamed, has held back the impulse toward fornication or uncleanness.
